name: Float
tagline: A team resource scheduler: who is booked on what, for how many hours, across which weeks.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Underneath the polish, Float is a grid: people down the side, days across the top, allocations in the cells, and arithmetic that tells you who is over capacity. That is a weekend build with SQLite and a drag-resizable timeline, and for a team of five it genuinely works. What does not come free is the part agencies actually buy: live multi-user editing without two schedulers clobbering each other, mobile access for people who are not at a desk, and the Jira/Asana/Slack/calendar plumbing that keeps the grid honest without manual entry. Float also gets drag-and-drop right in a way that takes weeks to approximate, and scheduling UI is exactly where sloppiness becomes unusable. Build it if you are the only scheduler and the team is small; buy it the moment two people need to edit the same week.
coreLoopDIY: A local timeline grid where you create people and projects, drag allocations onto days, and see per-person utilization and over-capacity warnings.
requirements: Node 20 and a local SQLite file
Manual entry of people, projects and hours since there is no PM tool sync
A single scheduler, or discipline about who edits when
A desktop browser; the grid will not be usable on a phone
whatYouLose: Real-time multi-user editing with conflict handling; concurrent edits will silently overwrite
Native mobile and tablet apps for people checking their own schedule
Integrations with Jira, Asana, Trello, Slack and calendars, so the grid drifts from reality
Time tracking against scheduled hours, and the reports that compare planned to actual
Drag-and-drop that feels right: snapping, multi-select, nudging, undo, bulk shifts
moatNotes: Scheduling tools live or die on whether a second person can touch the same week without chaos. That is a sync problem, not a UI problem.
whyPeopleStillPay: Float is bought by agencies and studios where the schedule is a shared source of truth, not one person's spreadsheet. Account leads, PMs and the people being booked all look at it, often at once, often from phones, and it has to match what is in the project tracker and the time sheets. A personal clone gives you the math and the picture; it does not give you fifteen other people trusting the picture. The subscription is mostly buying agreement across a team, plus the integration surface that keeps the agreement accurate.
notes: The grid is a weekend; the grid that five people edit at once is not.
prompt:
Build a local resource scheduling app called Shoal. One user, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Next.js 14 App Router with TypeScript
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/shoal.db, schema created on first run
- Tailwind CSS for styling
- No auth, no external APIs, no analytics

Data model:
- Person: id, name, role, weeklyCapacityHours (default 40), active
- Project: id, name, client, colorHex, archived
- Allocation: id, personId, projectId, startDate, endDate, hoursPerDay, note

Core screen, the Schedule:
- Rows are people, columns are days, horizontally scrollable, default view 4 weeks starting this Monday
- Weekends visually dimmed and excluded from capacity math
- Allocations render as colored bars spanning their date range, labeled with project name and hoursPerDay
- Click an empty cell to create an allocation in a modal: project, hours per day, end date, note
- Drag a bar left or right to move it, drag either edge to resize, snap to whole days, persist on drop
- Per-person per-day total hours; cells over capacity/5 get a red outline and the person row shows an over-capacity badge
- Keyboard: Delete removes the selected bar, Cmd+Z undoes the last create, move, resize or delete (keep a 20-step in-memory undo stack)

Second screen, Utilization:
- Per person, for the visible range: scheduled hours, capacity hours, percent utilized, in a plain table
- Per project: total scheduled hours and headcount
- CSV export of both tables

Also:
- People and Projects CRUD pages, nothing fancy
- Seed script with 6 people, 5 projects and a few weeks of plausible allocations
- README with setup commands and one paragraph on what this does not do: no mobile, no multi-user, no time tracking, no integrations

Out of scope, do not build: login, invites, sharing links, email, Slack or Jira sync, mobile layout, recurring allocations, time off approval workflows.
